title: A Simple Craft Your Credo Classroom Activity
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart documents a three-day, ten-minutes-a-day activity in which ninth graders draft I believe statements, read a short text set of real credos, and then write a final draft to be returned to them a month later for reflection. The write-up is structured as a comparison: the three-day version worked in two classes, while a compressed twelve-minute version attempted with a new advisory group did not. He is explicit about why the compressed attempt failed, citing his own rushed explanation, insufficient time, and credos of markedly lower quality, and he draws the generalisable lesson that quality learning experiences should be as quick as they can be but not quicker. He also sets the activity in its real context, running alongside a reading of Things Fall Apart that sits outside the standard curriculum, and he concedes he made no attempt to connect the novel to the credo work. The closing section handles the obvious objection, with Stuart stating that he is not a moral relativist and finds some student beliefs foolish or harmful, but arguing that the purpose is clarification rather than instruction in what to believe. His underlying claim is that everyone operates from a belief system and too few know what theirs is. The piece ends with the payoff he reports from reading the credos themselves.
points: The three-day structure matters more than the prompts: ten minutes to draft, ten minutes to read a text set of real credos and revise, ten minutes to produce a final draft, with the papers returned a month later for reflection.

Stuart's controlled failure is the most useful part of the record, since running the same activity in twelve minutes with a new group produced confusion and superficial credos, yielding the rule that learning experiences should be as quick as they can be but not quicker.
He is candid that class culture is a precondition, attributing the weaker result partly to having met the advisory group only four times.
The text set does the pedagogical heavy lifting by giving students real models, including a pope's credo and a company credo that cost it a hundred million dollars.
He explicitly rejects relativism while keeping a light hand, arguing that the aim is to help students articulate the belief system they already operate from rather than to install one.
quotes: This past week allowed me the opportunity to experiment with leading three groups of my students in a Craft Your Credo classroom activity, and I'd like to share that activity with you today. Two of the groups went quite well, and one didn't.

Anyway, the point is that this week, each day has kind of gone like this: 40-50 minutes for discussing and reading the novel, and 10-20 minutes for Something Else. Something Else is usually exam review, but the past few days Something Else has been credo crafting.
Some students complete the writing task in five minutes, and others take fifteen. The reading assignment at the end of the writing allows kids to take their time and produce their best work.

Surprise: it didn't work that well. Some students were confused (my explanation was rushed); most kids didn't have enough time (i.e., they did understand the activity, and as a result needed to put a bit of thought into it); and most of the credos were of a markedly different quality than those crafted using the three-day method described above.

Before I let you go, I want to clarify that I am not a moral or philosophical relativist. Some of the things my students write in their credos I find to be not just disagreeable, but even foolish or harmful. It's unfashionable to say so, but I think there are wise, helpful beliefs, and there are short-sighted, goal-hindering ones.

Every human being operates from a belief system about the world; too few actually know what their belief system is. In prompting my students to reflect, I am hoping to help them clarify their thinking about the things they hold true.
